strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a genuine gap in the typographic-attack literature: prior work and defenses focus almost exclusively on object-recognition robustness by encouraging text-ignoring, which is misaligned with real-world settings requiring joint object+text reasoning (e.g., autonomous driving, embodied agents).

The core benchmark design—same-scene counterfactuals crossing question type (object/text) x attack condition (clean/attacked)—is a clean and well-motivated experimental control that isolates selective text-use ability from confounds such as scene difference, which is a clear improvement over naively combining separate object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Substantial engineering effort in benchmark construction: hierarchical negative/attack-word sampling using the Open Images class hierarchy for object questions, LLM-generated contradictory but plausible attack phrases for open-ended text-VQA (a reportedly first attempt), and distance-controlled placement relative to key text regions and OCR boxes to avoid trivial or impossible attacks.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: six LVLMs of varying architectures/scales, multiple attack difficulty levels, two representative defenses (CoT, IT-RT) plus the proposed RIO-RT, detailed per-level breakdowns (Table 1), attention-map visualizations offering some mechanistic insight, LoRA placement ablation suggesting selective text use is primarily driven by the language component, and generalization experiments to external datasets (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA).

Provides a novel evaluation metric (Robust-CLIP-Match) tailored to jointly capture correctness and attack-resistance in open-ended object recognition, and clearly documents reproducibility details (prompts, hyperparameters, compute cost) in the appendix.

The proposed RIO-RT defense, despite being a relatively simple SFT recipe, is shown empirically to achieve a more balanced trade-off than the ignore-text baseline (IT-RT) and inference-time CoT prompting, providing a concrete, actionable outcome from the benchmark's training split.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely from a single source (TextVQA over Open Images); while the paper argues the pipeline generalizes to other dual-annotation datasets, this is not empirically demonstrated—only downstream generalization of the trained defense is tested, not benchmark construction on a second dataset, so the core claim of a broadly applicable pipeline rests partly on assertion.

Several automatic construction choices are not validated against human judgment: ground-truth object class selection uses CLIP top-1 similarity (which can be noisy or ambiguous for multi-label images), and LLM-generated (Llama-3) contradictory attack phrases for Text-Attack are not verified for quality, naturalness, or actual difficulty via human annotators, raising concerns about label noise and attack validity underlying the reported accuracy numbers.

The proposed defense (RIO-RT) is architecturally simple—balanced SFT mixture of Obj-Attack and Text-Attack samples—which, while effective, is a fairly incremental methodological contribution relative to the benchmark itself; the paper's main technical novelty is concentrated in benchmark/task design rather than the defense algorithm.

Baseline defense comparisons are somewhat narrow: only CoT prompting and a self-constructed IT-RT baseline are compared; existing published methods such as Defense-Prefix or CLIP-mirror-based approaches ([2],[39]) are not directly adapted and compared quantitatively (only discussed qualitatively as inapplicable to LVLMs), which limits the strength of claims that all existing defenses fail at this task.

The R-CLIP-M metric, while a reasonable proxy, is a similarity-based automatic metric that may not perfectly track human-perceived correctness or attack susceptibility, and no human evaluation or correlation study is provided to validate it.

Some claims of novelty (e.g., "first attempt" at open-ended text-VQA typographic attacks, "first structural foundation for training-based defenses") are somewhat strong given the relatively narrow technical departure from prior attack/defense formulations, and could be tempered.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated task formulation (RIO-VQA) that identifies a genuine blind spot in existing typographic-attack robustness evaluation: current object-centric protocols cannot distinguish 'true robustness' from indiscriminate text-suppression.

The same-scene counterfactual design (fixing the scene, varying only question intent and text condition) is a clean and effective methodological choice that meaningfully reduces confounds compared to naively combining separate object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Thorough and carefully engineered benchmark construction: hierarchical negative sampling for MC options, LLM-generated contradiction-based attacks for text-VQA, two complementary attack realism levels (controlled overlay and SceneTAP-based scene-coherent insertion with OCR-region safeguards), and a new R-CLIP-M metric that explicitly penalizes attack-word-induced bias in open-ended predictions.

Solid empirical validation of dataset quality via human audits with reasonable inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 0.89-0.94), which supports the claim that observed failures reflect genuine model behavior rather than dataset artifacts.

Broad and modern experimental coverage: 6 LVLM architectures/scales plus additional evaluation on newer open-source families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5) and closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro), along with multiple defense baselines (CoT, IT-RT, RIO-RT).

Insightful supporting analyses beyond the main benchmark results: attack-difficulty-level ablations, LoRA parameter-placement ablation (showing language-side adaptation matters most), attention-map visualizations that provide a plausible mechanistic explanation of the read/ignore behavior, and generalization checks to Typo-D and external text-VQA benchmarks.

The central finding (object-centric defenses gain robustness at the cost of text-reading, while balanced training mitigates this) is clearly demonstrated and has real significance for how the field should evaluate and design typographic-attack defenses.
weaknesses: The benchmark is derived entirely from a single source dataset (TextVQA/Open Images); scene diversity, image domains, and text types are therefore constrained, and it remains unclear how well findings transfer to substantially different real-world settings mentioned as motivation (e.g., traffic signs, embodied-agent instructions) beyond the limited external generalization experiments provided.

RIO-RT, the proposed defense, is essentially a straightforward SFT baseline on a balanced attack mixture; the algorithmic novelty is modest, and the paper explicitly frames it as a minimal reference rather than a fully developed defense, which is reasonable but limits the technical contribution beyond the benchmark itself.

Some quantitative results are only partially explained: e.g., the divergence between RIO-Bench text-degradation and preserved external text-VQA performance for LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision under IT-RT is interesting but only briefly discussed, leaving open questions about the generality of the 'domain-specific trade-off' claim.

The comparison against prior defenses is limited to a single LVLM-focused method (CoT) plus the paper's own two baselines, since most prior CLIP-centric defenses are not directly applicable; while this is justified, it somewhat narrows the empirical contrast against the broader defense literature.

The human audit, while showing strong agreement, is based on a relatively small sample (400 out of tens of thousands of instances), which may not fully capture rarer failure modes such as edge cases in attack-word plausibility or occasional over-strong/unanswerable text attacks.

The R-CLIP-M metric and CLIP-based ground-truth label selection introduce dependence on CLIP's own biases and similarity judgments, which could subtly affect both benchmark construction (label selection, negative sampling) and evaluation in ways not fully explored.
